narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'a reproach, dreaded, fled from', and the type (102) is state — cherpah here is not an act the self performs but a condition it falls into. The bearer (105) is the psalmist, and the operation (106) traces the movement in full: 'because of adversaries the self has become a reproach, an object of dread to acquaintances, fled from in the street — the pain of social rejection.' The target (107) is social-shame: the reproach is directed outward into the arena of neighbours, acquaintances and passers-by, and it is there that the interior is wounded. Coupling (112) welds it to being shunned ('reproach-shunned') — the shame and the withdrawal of others are one linked event. Source is not recorded (103 present:false): the passage names the adversaries as occasion but registers no originating cause inside the item itself; the reproach simply lands. Seat is 'none' (104) and locus (116) is internal:ib-state — this is not lodged in an organ but is a state of the whole self, felt inwardly even as its cause is outward. Manner is 'none' (108): no mode is described. Intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are all absent (109/110/111/113 present:false): the reader measures no degree of the shame, adds no qualifier, traces no downstream consequence, and does not frame it as forbidden — the state is reported, not graded or resolved. Role (115) is characteristic. The discovery (114) fixes it: 'I have become a reproach... an object of dread to my acquaintances; those who see me in the street flee from me' — the interior suffers the withdrawal of everyone. Read for the inner being, reproach here is the wound of being made repellent to one's own community — the self experiences its own diminishment through the eyes of those who flee it.
narratives.story: David describes a specific kind of pain: he has become someone people are ashamed to be near. Because of those attacking him, his neighbours dread him and his old friends look away; when people see him in the street they hurry off in the other direction. He has not done anything here — this is something that has happened to him, a condition he has sunk into rather than a choice he made. The hurt is not in any one part of his body but sits deep inside, the ache of watching everyone withdraw. It is the loneliness of a person who feels he has become repellent to the very community he belonged to.
narratives.variation_note: Of the three reproach (cherpah) readings this is the only one where the reproach is a purely social wound turned inward (target social-shame, locus internal:ib-state) with no reference to God: the self becomes repellent to its community. By contrast #2 (69:7) and #3 (69:9) read the reproach as borne for God's sake with locus external:god — shame suffered on God's account rather than the pain of communal rejection.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'reproach (cherpah — for your sake I have borne reproach)', and the type (102) is status — a standing the psalmist occupies rather than a passing feeling. The bearer (105) is the psalmist, and the operation (106) is 'borne / carried': crucially this is an active endurance, the self shouldering a load, not merely sinking into a condition. The target (107) is 'for God's sake' — the whole vector of the reproach points toward God as its reason, which is why the locus (116) is external:god: the shame reaches outside the self and is bound up with God's own honour. Manner (108) is a pair (spans 281896->281897): the reproach is borne with 'dishonor covering his face', shame's outward mark. Coupling (112) is a pair (281896->281905) tying it to 'the reproaches that fell on him for God (v9)' — this reading anticipates and links to reading #3. Source is not recorded (103 present:false): no cause internal to the item is named; the reproach's origin lies in his devotion, stated as target rather than source. Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-located. Intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are absent (109/110/111/113): no degree, qualifier, consequence or prohibition is registered — the endurance is stated without being measured or resolved. Role (115) is characteristic. The discovery (114) reads it as 'shame suffered on God's account... his disgrace bound up with God's.' For the inner being, reproach here is a chosen, borne shame — the self willingly carries humiliation because its life is fastened to God, transfiguring disgrace into an act of loyalty.
narratives.story: Here the psalmist owns his shame in a different way: he carries it deliberately, and he carries it because of God. The insults heaped on him are not random misfortune but the cost of belonging to God, and he shoulders them the way a man carries a heavy load he has agreed to bear. The disgrace shows on him like a covering over his face, and it is knotted together with the wider scorn that falls on him for God's sake. What could have crushed him he instead takes up as loyalty. His humiliation points away from himself and toward the God whose honour he shares.
narratives.variation_note: Differs from #1 (31:11) in that the reproach is not the inward pain of social rejection but a status actively borne for God (target 'for God's sake', locus external:god, operation 'borne/carried'). It differs from #3 (69:9) in direction: here the psalmist carries the reproach as his own devotional burden, whereas #3 reads reproaches originally aimed at God falling onto him — endurance chosen vs. scorn received.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'reproaches (cherpah — the reproaches of those who reproach you fell on me)', and the type (102) is status. The bearer (105) is the psalmist, but the operation (106) is distinctive: 'fall on him' (a pair, spans 281905->281907) — the reproach is received, landing on the self from elsewhere rather than actively shouldered. The target (107) is the key finding: 'originally aimed at God' — the scorn was launched at God and lands on his servant, so the movement runs God -> reviler -> psalmist. Accordingly the locus (116) is external:god: the reproach belongs to God's sphere and only secondarily settles on the man. Coupling (112) is a pair (281905->281896) binding it back to 'the reproach borne for God (v7)', linking this reading to #2. Source is not recorded (103 present:false): no separate cause is named; the reviling of God is itself the well from which it comes, captured under target. Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-lodged. Manner is 'none' (108). Intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are absent (109/110/111/113): the reader records no measured degree, no qualifier, no traced consequence, and no prohibition. Role (115) is characteristic. The discovery (114) is pointed: 'the insults hurled at God landing on his servant... identification with God so complete that God's shame becomes his (cited Rom 15:3).' For the inner being, this reproach reveals a self so fused to God that the abuse meant for God is absorbed into the person's own interior — shame received by proxy, the price of total identification.
narratives.story: The mockery here was never really aimed at the psalmist first — it was aimed at God, and it simply lands on him because he stands so close to God. Insults thrown at heaven fall on the man beneath. He does not go looking to carry them; they come down on him because he and God have become inseparable in the eyes of the scoffers. When he wept and fasted, even that was turned into more scorn. His identification with God is so complete that God's disgrace becomes his own, absorbed straight into his heart.
narratives.variation_note: Against #2 (69:7), where the psalmist actively bears reproach 'for God's sake' (operation 'borne/carried', target 'for God's sake'), this reading has the reproach 'fall on him' with target 'originally aimed at God' — scorn received by proxy rather than chosen and shouldered. Both share locus external:god, but the direction of the movement differs: #2 the self reaches toward God's honour, #3 God's disgrace descends onto the self. Against #1 (31:11) both differ wholly: #1 is inward social shame, these are shame tied to God.

narratives.narrative: This is the family's single ascent reading, and the sense (101) is 'those who look to him are radiant'. The type (102) is affect — a felt, luminous interior state, not an act or a mere status. The bearer (105) is 'those who look to him', a plural of the trusting, and the operation (106) is transformation by gaze: 'those who look to God are radiant, their faces never ashamed — the interior lit up by looking to him.' The target (107) is 'radiance' itself: the movement issues in an inner light that surfaces on the face. Coupling (112) welds the two halves into a single mechanism, 'look-and-be-radiant' — the looking and the shining are one linked motion. Source is not recorded (103 present:false): no external agent is named as igniting the radiance; it arises from the act of looking, which the reading treats as target/operation rather than as an outside source. Seat is 'none' (104) and locus (116) is internal:ib-state — this is not organ-lodged but a condition of the whole self. Manner is 'none' (108): no mode described. Intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are absent (109/110/111/113 present:false): the reader records no degree of brightness, no qualifier, no separately traced consequence, and no prohibition — the shining is simply stated. Role (115) is characteristic. The discovery (114) crystallises it: 'transformation by gaze: the interior that turns to God is lit and kept from shame.' Read for the inner being, radiance is the exact inverse of the family's shame movements — where reproach and disgrace darken and cover the face, here the outward-turned gaze floods the interior with light and the face is guaranteed against shame. Shame is here defeated not by rescue after the fact but by the direction of attention.
narratives.story: In the middle of a family of poems all about shame, this one line shines the other way. People who turn their eyes toward God light up inside, and that inner light shows on their faces so that they are never left disgraced. It is not that God rescues them from shame after it strikes — it is that the simple act of looking to him fills them and keeps shame from ever settling. The looking and the shining are the same motion. Where the others describe faces covered and heads bowed, here the face is lifted and glowing.
narratives.variation_note: The only reading in the family; also its only positive movement. Where every shame item traces a covering, wrapping or bowing of the face, radiant reverses the vector: the outward gaze toward God produces inner light (type affect, target radiance) and pre-empts shame ('their faces shall never be ashamed'), making it the structural counterpoint to the whole shame-confusion set.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'shame (bosheth — covers my face)', and the type (102) is status — a settled condition the sufferer inhabits. The bearer (105) is the nation: this is a communal shame, 'us', not one man. The operation (106) is a pair (spans 278724->...) 'cover the face' — shame behaves like a veil drawn over the countenance, the visible seat of dignity. The manner (108) is a pair (278724->278730): the shame is felt 'at the taunter and avenger', i.e. in the presence of mocking and hostile onlookers, which supply its occasion. Coupling (112) is a pair (278724->278722) binding shame to disgrace ('paired with disgrace'), linking this reading to the kelimmah item alongside it in the same verse. Target is 'none' (107, resolution none): the shame does not aim outward at anyone — it settles on the self, a purely inward covering with no object. Source is not recorded (103 present:false): though the wider psalm names God's rejection (v9) as the deep cause, this bosheth item records no source, leaving the shame's origin unstated at the item level. Seat is 'none' (104) yet the operation and discovery both locate it on the face; locus (116) is internal:ib-state — the covering is an inner condition surfacing outwardly, not an organ. Intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are absent (109/110/111/113): no degree, qualifier, downstream consequence or prohibition is registered. Role (115) is characteristic. The discovery (114) reads it as 'shame as a veil over the countenance... the disgrace that covers the face at the sound of the taunter and reviler.' For the inner being, shame here is a communal covering — a whole people's dignity screened out by humiliation, felt inwardly with no outward target, simply endured before the jeering of enemies.
narratives.story: This is a whole community's shame, not one person's. All day long a sense of disgrace hangs over them, and shame is drawn across their faces like a veil, hiding the dignity a face is meant to show. It is not aimed at anyone — it just settles down over them and stays there. What brings it on is the sound of taunts and the sight of gloating enemies, whose mockery makes the covering fall. The people do nothing back; they simply carry the humiliation inwardly, faces hidden, under the jeering of those around them.
narratives.variation_note: Of the two bosheth ('shame') readings this one is self-suffered: the nation's own shame covers its face, with no target (107 none) and no bearer-as-enemy. The other, #2 (109:29), reverses it — shame is invoked upon the accusers, who are 'wrapped in shame as in a cloak', bearer = the accusers. Here shame descends on the sufferer; there it is called down on the foe.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'disgrace / humiliation (kelimmah)', and the type (102) is status. Uniquely in this family, source IS recorded (103): a pair (spans 278722->278857) names 'God's rejecting and disgracing (v9)' — the deep origin of the humiliation is traced back to God's own act of casting off, an uncomfortable finding the reading does not soften. The bearer (105) is the nation ('my disgrace'). The operation (106) is 'none' (resolution none): notably, no verb-action is attached — the disgrace does not do anything or move; it simply stands. This is confirmed by target (107) 'none': it aims nowhere. Instead the manner (108) carries the weight: 'all day long before me' — the humiliation's mode is relentless, ceaseless presence in the sufferer's sight. Coupling (112) is a pair (278722->278724) 'paired with shame covering the face', binding it to the bosheth item beside it. Seat is 'none' (104) and locus (116) internal:ib-state — an inner condition, not organ-lodged. Intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are absent (109/110/111/113): the disgrace is neither graded, qualified, given a consequence, nor forbidden. Role (115) is characteristic. The discovery (114) reads it as 'the humiliation constantly in view; kelimmah the shame the nation carries, its source God's rejecting and disgracing (v9 qualifier), the taunter and reviler its occasion.' For the inner being, disgrace here is a static, ever-present interior weight whose ultimate author, the reading dares to say, is God himself — the community's shame is not merely the enemies' doing but the felt outcome of divine rejection, held constantly before the mind's eye with no movement and no relief.
narratives.story: Alongside the veil of shame in the same verse sits a heavier thing: disgrace that never moves and never leaves. It does not act or reach out; it just stands there, in front of the people every waking hour, all day long. And the poem does something startling — it traces this humiliation not only to the mocking enemies but back to God, who has cast his people off. The taunters are only the occasion; the real source is a God who seems to have turned away. The disgrace simply sits before them, a constant weight on the mind, with no relief in sight.
narratives.variation_note: The only kelimmah 'disgrace' reading; the sole item in the family to record a source (103), and it names God's own rejecting and disgracing (v9) as origin. It is also distinctive for having no operation and no target (both 'none') — a static, motionless humiliation whose whole force is carried by its manner, 'all day long before me'. Distinguished from the paired bosheth (#1) in the same verse: shame covers the face (an act), disgrace merely stands in view (a state).

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'be put to shame (bosh — you put them to shame)', and the type (102) is status. Source IS recorded (103): a pair (spans 279936->279939) names 'because God has rejected them (v5)' — the shame of the godless is grounded in God's prior rejection. The bearer (105) is 'the evildoers' — this is a descent reading, the interior of the wicked, read (per directive 5) with the same weight as any sufferer's. The operation (106) is 'be put to shame' (inferred), a passive undergoing: the fools who said 'there is no God' are made to bear disgrace. Target is 'none' (107, resolution none): the shame does not reach outward but collapses inward on them. Coupling (112) is a pair (279936->279928) 'paired with their terror' — the shame is welded to the great dread that seizes them 'where there is no terror', so exposure and panic are one event. Seat is 'none' (104) and locus (116) internal:ib-state — the ruin is interior, not organ-lodged. Manner is 'none' (108). Intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are absent (109/110/111/113): no degree, qualifier, traced consequence or prohibition. Role (115) is characteristic. The discovery (114) reads it as 'the disgrace of the godless when their confidence collapses... the inner ruin of exposure and defeat, grounded in God's rejection of them.' For the inner being, this is shame as the interior undoing of the self-assured wicked: the ones who denied God are stripped of their false confidence, their bravado dissolving into terror and disgrace precisely because God has rejected them — the collapse of a godless interior from the inside out.
narratives.story: The poem watches what happens inside people who told themselves there is no God. Their swagger falls apart. Sudden terror grips them even where nothing frightening is present, and with it comes disgrace — they are exposed and defeated from the inside. And the reason given is stark: God has rejected them, and that rejection is the ground of their collapse. The confidence they built on denying God simply caves in, leaving panic and shame where certainty used to be. It is the undoing of a self-assured heart that had no room for God.
narratives.variation_note: This bosh reading (char_key putthemtosham, distinct from puttosham) is a descent reading focused on the interior collapse of the wicked, and it records a source (103): 'because God has rejected them'. Its coupling to terror (112) marks it out — shame here is fused with panic, the inner ruin of exposed godlessness, rather than the vindication-shame invoked on enemies elsewhere in the family.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'dishonor / shame (kelimmah — dishonor has covered my face)', and the type (102) is status. The bearer (105) is the psalmist. Distinctively, seat IS recorded (104): 'the face' — this reading lodges the dishonor on a specific bodily site, the countenance, the visible register of a person's standing. The operation (106) is 'cover his face' (inferred): the shame behaves like a garment drawn over the face. Target is 'none' (107): the dishonor does not aim outward but settles inward. Coupling (112) is a pair (spans 281897->281896) 'paired with the reproach borne for God', binding this item to the cherpah of the same verse (reading #2) — dishonor is the visible mark of the reproach. Source is not recorded (103 present:false): no separate origin is named at the item level; the covering is stated as fact. Manner is 'none' (108). Locus (116) is internal:ib-state: though it rests on the face, the dishonor is an inner condition surfacing outwardly. Intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are absent (109/110/111/113): no degree, qualifier, traced consequence or prohibition. Role (115) is characteristic. The discovery (114) reads it as 'humiliation veiling the psalmist like a garment... the visible mark of the reproach borne for God's sake.' For the inner being, dishonor here is the outward face of an inwardly borne shame: what the psalmist carries within (the reproach for God) shows itself as a covering over his face — the interior humiliation made visible, seated on the countenance for all to see.
narratives.story: The shame the psalmist carries for God's sake does not stay hidden — it shows on his face. Dishonour has come down over his features like a cloth pulled across them, the visible sign of everything he is bearing within. It does not lash out at anyone; it simply settles on him, resting on the very part of a person where dignity usually shows. This covering of the face is the outward mark of the reproach he shoulders because he belongs to God. What he suffers inside has surfaced for everyone to see.
narratives.variation_note: Of the two kelimmah 'dishonor' readings this one is self-suffered and, uniquely, seats the shame on 'the face' (104) — the psalmist's own humiliation made visible as the outward mark of reproach borne for God. The other, #2 (109:29), reverses the bearer: dishonor is invoked upon the accusers, 'clothed with dishonor', with seat 'none'. Here the face wears shame; there enemies are dressed in it as a called-down garment.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'downtrodden / crushed (dak — let not the downtrodden turn back in shame)', and the type (102) is status — a crushed condition, not an act. Source IS recorded (103): a pair (spans 282619->282522) identifies these as those 'whom God is implored not to cast off (v1)', tracing the plea back to the psalm's opening cry against divine abandonment. The bearer (105) is 'the downtrodden' — the oppressed, beaten-down community. The operation (106) is unusual for the family: 'be kept from turning back in shame' (inferred) — the movement is a prayer that shame be averted, that the crushed not slink away disgraced. The manner (108) is a pair (282619->282621) 'not turned back in shame', reinforcing that the feared motion is a shamed retreat. Target is 'none' (107): the state aims nowhere outward. Coupling (112) is a pair (282619->282622) 'paired with the poor and needy who praise God' — the downtrodden are set beside those who, vindicated, praise; the alternative to shamed retreat is grateful praise. Seat is 'none' (104) and locus (116) internal:ib-state. Intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are absent (109/110/111/113): no degree, qualifier, consequence or prohibition. Role (115) is characteristic. The discovery (114) reads it as 'the crushed people the psalmist pleads for... whom he begs God not to let go away disgraced.' For the inner being, the downtrodden state is a crushed interior teetering on the edge of shamed withdrawal; the reading captures the pivot point where the oppressed self either retreats humiliated or is lifted to praise — and the whole weight of the prayer is that God tip it toward the latter.
narratives.story: The prayer is for people who have been beaten down and worn out, the crushed and the poor of a battered community. The fear is that they will simply turn away in shame — slink off defeated, humiliated by all they have suffered. So the psalmist begs God not to let that happen, tying the plea back to his earlier cry that God not cast his people off. He sets two futures side by side: the crushed retreating in disgrace, or the same poor and needy people lifting their voices in praise. Everything hangs on which way God lets it fall.
narratives.variation_note: The only reading of dak 'downtrodden'; distinctive in that the shame is not present but feared and prayed against — the operation is 'be kept from turning back in shame' rather than a shame undergone or invoked. It records a source (103) reaching back to the psalm's plea against God's casting-off, and couples the crushed to the praising poor (112), framing a pivot between shamed retreat and vindicated praise.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'become a reproach (cherpah)', and the type (102) is state — a condition entered, not an act performed. The bearer (105) is 'we (the people)' — a communal reproach, the whole nation. The operation (106) is 'become an object of scorn': the self does not do anything but is transformed into a thing others deride. The target (107) is 'to the neighbours': the reproach is registered in the eyes of surrounding peoples, the arena where the shame lands. Coupling (112) welds it to 'being mocked and derided' — the reproach and the active mockery of neighbours are one linked event. Source is not recorded (103 present:false): no originating cause is named at the item level, though the psalm's wider setting is national catastrophe; the reproach is stated as an accomplished condition. Seat is 'none' (104) and locus (116) internal:ib-state — a state of the corporate self, not organ-lodged. Manner is 'none' (108). Intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are absent (109/110/111/113): no degree, qualifier, traced consequence or prohibition. Role (115) is characteristic. The discovery (114) reads it as 'the communal humiliation, the shame of a people whose God seems to have abandoned them; disgrace felt as an inner wound.' For the inner being, becoming a reproach is the corporate self experiencing its own transformation into an object of contempt — the community's identity collapsed from a people into a byword, the shame felt inwardly as a wound even as its stage is the surrounding nations.
narratives.story: A whole people speaks here, and what they say is that they have turned into a joke. To the nations around them they have become a thing to sneer at, mocked and laughed down on every side. They did not do anything to earn this in the moment — they simply became it, their standing as a people collapsing into contempt. Underneath the taunts is the deeper ache that their God seems to have walked away from them. The scorn happens out in the open, before the neighbours, but the wound of it is felt deep inside the community's shared heart.
narratives.variation_note: Of the two cherpah 'become' readings this one is communal: the bearer is 'we (the people)', a whole nation becoming a byword to its neighbours. The other, #2 (89:41), narrows the bearer to a single figure, 'the king' / the anointed. Same verb and movement (become a reproach/scorn), same target-arena (the neighbours), but corporate shame here versus the humiliation of the individual anointed there.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'become a scorn (cherpah)', and the type (102) is state. The bearer (105) is 'the king' — the anointed of the covenant, whose downfall the psalm laments. The operation (106) is simply 'become': the king does not act but is reduced, plundered by all who pass, into an object of scorn. The target (107) is 'a scorn to his neighbours' — the humiliation is registered before surrounding peoples. The recorded coupling (112) and locus (116) values are cross-filed here: the coupling flag carries 'internal:ib-state' while the locus value reads 'paired with the enemies' rejoicing' — read for substance, the scorn is an inner state of the king that is set beside the exultation of his foes (v42, 'you have made all his enemies rejoice'), so his disgrace and their gladness are one contrasted event. Source is not recorded (103 present:false): though the psalm lays the whole ruin at God's door ('you have cast off and rejected', v38), this item names no source, leaving the origin unstated at the item level. Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-lodged. Manner is 'none' (108). Intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are absent (109/110/111/113): no degree, qualifier, consequence or prohibition. Role (115) is characteristic. The discovery (114) reads it as 'the king's humiliation, the anointed made a reproach.' For the inner being, this is the collapse of the highest human standing into contempt: the crowned self, once secured by covenant, becomes a plundered byword — inner honour stripped and set against the mocking joy of enemies.
narratives.story: Here it is a king who has become a laughingstock. Once crowned and secured by promise, he is now plundered by everyone who walks past, reduced to something his neighbours sneer at. His disgrace is made sharper by what stands next to it — his enemies are cheering, rejoicing over his fall, so his shame and their triumph are held up together. The poem grieves that all of this has come from God's own turning away. The man at the very top has been brought as low as it goes, his honour stripped off him for the crowds to jeer at.
narratives.variation_note: Against #1 (79:4) this narrows the bearer from 'we (the people)' to a single figure, the king / anointed, and contrasts his scorn with the enemies' rejoicing rather than pairing it with generalised mockery. Note the data files coupling and locus with crossed values here (coupling='internal:ib-state', locus='paired with the enemies' rejoicing'); read for substance, the king's inner disgrace is set against his foes' exultation.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'shame (bushah)', and the type (102) is state. The bearer (105) is 'the king' — the same anointed figure whose ruin the psalm mourns. The operation (106) is 'be covered with shame' — a passive undergoing, shame drawn over him like a garment. The target (107) is the uncomfortable finding: 'by God' — it is God who covers the king with shame. This makes God the agent of the humiliation, and the reading, per directive 6, does not soften it: the divine hand that once promised steadfast love now clothes its anointed in disgrace. Coupling (112) ties the shame to 'the days of his youth cut short' — the humiliation is welded to a premature ruin, honour and vigour ended together. Source is not recorded (103 present:false) at the item level even though target names God as agent; the origin is carried under target rather than source. Seat is 'none' (104) and locus (116) internal:ib-state — an inner condition, not organ-lodged. Manner is 'none' (108). Intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are absent (109/110/111/113): no degree, qualifier, traced consequence or prohibition. Role (115) is characteristic. The discovery (114) reads it as 'the disgrace laid on the anointed, glory turned to humiliation.' For the inner being, this shame is a divinely-imposed covering: the king's interior glory is not merely lost to enemies but actively veiled by God himself — the highest human dignity overturned by the very One who conferred it, an interior emptied of honour by divine act.
narratives.story: The king's shame here has a hard edge the others do not: it is God himself who has covered him with it. The One who had promised to keep faith with him has instead drawn disgrace over him like a cloak, and cut his best years short at the same time. Glory has been turned into humiliation by the very hand that gave the glory. The poem does not look away from how painful and puzzling this is. The anointed one sits emptied of honour, and the source of that emptying is not just his enemies but his God.
narratives.variation_note: The only reading of bushah 'shame'; distinctive because the agent of the shame (target 107) is 'by God' — God himself covers the king with disgrace, the family's starkest instance of divinely-imposed shame (paralleling the source-as-God findings at 44:15 and 53:5). It is coupled not to enemy mockery but to 'the days of his youth cut short', binding humiliation to premature ruin.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'be put to shame (bosh)', and the type (102) is state. The bearer (105) is 'the enemies' — the confederate nations arrayed against God's people; this is a descent reading, the interior of the foe. The operation (106) is 'be put to shame', a passive undergoing invoked by imprecation ('Let them be put to shame'). The target (107) is 'before God': the shaming happens in God's presence, its whole point being that they 'may seek your name' and 'know that you alone... are the Most High' (v16, 18). Coupling (112) welds the shame to 'being dismayed' — shame and terror-collapse are one event, and the psalm asks that both be 'forever'. Source is not recorded (103 present:false): the shame is prayed for rather than traced to an origin within the item. Seat is 'none' (104) and locus (116) internal:ib-state — the ruin is interior. Manner is 'none' (108). Intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are absent (109/110/111/113): no degree, qualifier, traced consequence or prohibition. Role (115) is characteristic. The discovery (114) reads it as 'the enemies' humiliation invoked, disgrace as the outcome of their enmity.' For the inner being, this is shame requested as a redemptive undoing: the psalmist prays that the foes' interiors collapse in disgrace and dismay not merely as punishment but so that, humiliated, they might turn and seek God — shame here is asked to break a hostile self open toward acknowledgement.
narratives.story: The prayer is bold: let the enemies be shamed. The psalmist asks God to fill their faces with disgrace and leave them dismayed, undone from the inside. But there is a striking twist in the reason — he wants their humiliation so that they will finally seek God's name and admit that he alone is the Most High. The shame is not only meant to crush them but to break them open, to turn hardened foes toward the God they defied. It is disgrace prayed for as a strange kind of mercy, the collapse of pride that might make room for worship.
narratives.variation_note: First of the seven bosh 'put to shame' (puttosham) readings. This is a descent reading with the enemies as bearer, shame invoked by imprecation, and — distinctively — a redemptive target ('before God', that they may seek his name). It couples shame to dismay (112) and asks it 'forever'. Contrast #5 (119:6), the sole ascent puttosham reading (the psalmist NOT put to shame), and the vindication readings #2/#4/#7 where enemies are shamed to vindicate the servant rather than to convert them.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'perish in disgrace (chapher)', and the type (102) is state. The bearer (105) is 'the enemies', the same confederates as the paired bosh item in this verse — and preserving the distinction between the two (directive 8) is the finding. The operation (106) is 'be disgraced', but the target (107) is 'and perish': this disgrace is not the convertible shame of the paired reading but a terminal one — humiliation bound to destruction. Coupling (112) ties it to 'the shame and dismay' of v17, so chapher completes a triad with bosh (shame) and dismay. Source is not recorded (103 present:false): the disgrace is invoked, not traced to an origin. Seat is 'none' (104) and locus (116) internal:ib-state. Manner is 'none' (108). Intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are absent (109/110/111/113): no degree, qualifier, separately-traced consequence or prohibition — the perishing is carried under target rather than effect. Role (115) is characteristic. The discovery (114) reads it as 'the confounded end of the confederates, honour stripped away.' For the inner being, chapher is disgrace read as an end-state: where the paired bosh (#puttosham#1) holds open the possibility that shame might turn the foes to seek God, chapher fastens humiliation to perishing — the interior confounded not toward acknowledgement but toward its own extinction. The same verse thus holds two disgraces that must not be collapsed: one that might convert, one that consummates ruin.
narratives.story: In the very same line where the enemies are asked to be shamed so they might seek God, a second, darker word appears: let them perish in disgrace. This is humiliation with no way out — shame tied to destruction, honour stripped off as they go down. It stands right beside the more hopeful shame, and the two must not be blurred into one. One kind of disgrace might break a proud heart open toward God; this kind simply confounds and finishes. The psalmist holds both together, asking that the enemies' pride be undone whether toward worship or toward their end.
narratives.variation_note: The only reading of chapher 'disgrace'; must be held distinct from the bosh 'put to shame' item paired with it in the same verse (puttosham#1). Where that bosh is shame invoked so the foes may seek God, this chapher fastens disgrace to perishing (target 'and perish') — a terminal humiliation. Same bearer and verse, but one shame opens toward acknowledgement, the other consummates ruin.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'be put to shame (bosh)', and the type (102) is state. The bearer (105) is 'the haters' — the insolent, ruthless men who rose against the psalmist (v14). The operation (106) is 'be put to shame', a passive undergoing. The target (107) supplies the distinctive mechanism: 'by God's help to the psalmist' — the foes are shamed not by tempest or direct imprecation but by witnessing God's rescue of his servant ('that those who hate me may see and be put to shame because you, Lord, have helped me'). Coupling (112) welds the shame to 'the hatred' — the shame is the answer to their enmity, hatred turned back on itself. Source is not recorded (103 present:false): no origin is traced at the item level beyond the target's mechanism. Seat is 'none' (104) and locus (116) internal:ib-state. Manner is 'none' (108). Intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are absent (109/110/111/113): no degree, qualifier, traced consequence or prohibition. Role (115) is characteristic. The discovery (114) reads it as 'the confounding of the foes when God vindicates his servant.' For the inner being, this shame is the interior collapse produced by seeing another vindicated: the haters' confidence is undone not by a blow but by the sight of God's favour resting on the one they despised — shame as the deflation of enmity when its object is manifestly upheld.
narratives.story: The psalmist asks God for a visible sign of favour, and the point of it is what it will do to his enemies: when they see that God has helped and comforted him, they will be shamed. Their humiliation comes not from a storm or a curse but simply from watching the man they hated being upheld. Their own hatred is turned back on them, deflated by the plain sight of God's kindness to its target. It is the quiet undoing of people who despised someone, only to see God stand openly on his side. Their confidence caves in at the sight.
narratives.variation_note: Among the puttosham readings, this one's mechanism is distinctive: the foes are shamed 'by God's help to the psalmist' (target 107) — vindication-shame, produced by their seeing the servant upheld, and coupled to 'the hatred' rather than to dismay (#1) or terror. Unlike #1 (83:17) the aim is not their conversion but the deflation of their enmity; it shares with #4 (109:28) and #7 (129:5) the vindication logic but here it turns specifically on witnessing God's favour.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'put to shame (bosh)', and the type (102) is state. The bearer (105) is 'the idolaters' — 'all worshipers of images... who make their boast in worthless idols'. The operation (106) is 'be put to shame', a passive undergoing triggered by theophany: as the LORD appears in glory, the mountains melting like wax (v5), the image-worshippers are confounded. The target (107) is 'before the true God': the shaming happens in the presence of the manifest deity, exposing the emptiness of their boast. The recorded coupling (112) and locus (116) values are cross-filed here: the coupling flag reads 'internal:ib-state' while the locus value reads 'paired with worshipping images' — read for substance, the shame is an inner state welded to the very act of idolatry, so that their worship and their disgrace are one linked thing. Source is not recorded (103 present:false): no origin traced at item level beyond the theophany. Seat is 'none' (104). Manner is 'none' (108). Intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are absent (109/110/111/113): no degree, qualifier, consequence or prohibition. Role (115) is characteristic. The discovery (114) reads it as 'the confounding of idolaters when the true God appears.' For the inner being, this shame is the interior collapse of misplaced trust: those whose confidence rested on images find that confidence exposed as empty the moment the real God is revealed — the boast in nothing turns, in his presence, into disgrace. The self that leaned on idols is shamed by the mere fact of God's reality.
narratives.story: When God shows himself in glory, with the mountains melting like wax before him, the people who worshipped statues are left ashamed. They had boasted in their images as if those were something, and now, standing in the presence of the real God, that boast collapses into disgrace. Their shame is tied directly to their idol-worship — the very thing they trusted becomes the thing that humiliates them. It is not that God has to strike them; his simple reality is enough to expose the emptiness they leaned on. The confidence built on nothing falls apart the moment the true God appears.
narratives.variation_note: This puttosham reading's bearer is uniquely 'the idolaters', and the shaming is triggered by theophany, its target 'before the true God' — the exposure of misplaced trust when God appears, rather than the vindication of a servant (#2/#4/#7) or the imprecatory conversion-shame of #1. The data files coupling and locus with crossed values (coupling='internal:ib-state', locus='paired with worshipping images'); read for substance, the shame is welded to the act of idolatry itself.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'put to shame (bosh)', and the type (102) is state. The bearer (105) is 'the enemies'. The operation (106) is 'be put to shame', a passive undergoing. The target (107) is 'when they arise': the shame strikes precisely as they rise to curse — 'Let them curse, but you will bless! They arise and are put to shame' (v28) — so their aggressive motion turns into their disgrace. The recorded coupling (112) and locus (116) values are cross-filed here: the coupling flag reads 'internal:ib-state' while the locus value reads 'paired with the servant's gladness' — read for substance, the enemies' shame is an inner state set in sharp antithesis to the servant's joy, the two held in one balanced contrast (their shame / his gladness, their curse / God's blessing). Source is not recorded (103 present:false). Seat is 'none' (104). Manner is 'none' (108). Intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are absent (109/110/111/113): no degree, qualifier, traced consequence or prohibition. Role (115) is characteristic. The discovery (114) reads it as 'the foes shamed, the servant gladdened.' For the inner being, this shame is one pole of a two-sided reversal: the same divine action that turns the enemies' cursing into disgrace turns the servant's affliction into gladness — the interior of the foe collapses in shame in the very act of attack, while the interior of the servant is lifted. The reading holds both movements together as a single stroke of vindication.
narratives.story: The scene is a courtroom reversal. The enemies stand up to curse, but as they rise their curse turns into their own shame — God blesses where they meant to damn. And their disgrace is set right against something else: the servant's gladness. Their humiliation and his joy are two sides of the same moment, their cursing answered by God's blessing. The very act of attacking becomes the act of their undoing, while the one they attacked is lifted into gladness. It is a single stroke that shames the aggressors and rejoices the faithful.
narratives.variation_note: This puttosham reading is distinctive for its explicit antithesis: the enemies' shame is paired with the servant's gladness (the balanced curse/bless, shame/joy structure of v28), and the shame strikes 'when they arise' (target 107) — their aggressive motion itself becomes their disgrace. It shares vindication logic with #2 (86:17) and #7 (129:5) but is uniquely built as a two-pole reversal against the servant's joy. The data files coupling and locus with crossed values.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'shame (bosheth)', and the type (102) is state. The bearer (105) is 'the accusers'. The operation (106) is 'be wrapped in shame' — a garment-image, shame enveloping the self. The target (107) is 'as a cloak': 'may they be wrapped in their own shame as in a cloak' (v29), so the disgrace is worn, total, covering them entirely. The recorded coupling (112) and locus (116) values are cross-filed: the coupling flag reads 'internal:ib-state' while the locus value reads 'paired with the dishonor' — read for substance, the shame is an inner state welded to the kelimmah 'dishonor' of the same verse (reading #dishonor#2), the two garments of disgrace worn together. Source is not recorded (103 present:false): the shame is invoked, not traced to an origin. Seat is 'none' (104). Manner is 'none' (108). Intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are absent (109/110/111/113): no degree, qualifier, consequence or prohibition. Role (115) is characteristic. The discovery (114) reads it as 'the shame that covers the accusers, their own disgrace their clothing.' For the inner being, this shame is disgrace called down as total covering — the accusers' interior wrapped in humiliation as a man is wrapped in a robe, and pointedly 'their own shame', a disgrace that is theirs by right, issuing from their own accusing. The self that clothed itself in accusation is re-clothed in the shame that accusation earns.
narratives.story: The psalmist prays that his accusers be wrapped up in shame like a man wrapping himself in a cloak — total, head to foot, their disgrace worn as clothing. And it is called 'their own shame', the humiliation they have earned by their own accusing. Right beside it sits another word for disgrace, so they are dressed in shame twice over. The people who tried to clothe him in guilt end up clothed in disgrace themselves. What they aimed at him settles instead over them, covering them completely.
narratives.variation_note: Against #1 (44:15), where bosheth is the nation's own shame covering its face (self-suffered, no target), this reverses the bearer to 'the accusers' and the movement to imprecation: shame is called down on the foes and 'wrapped... as in a cloak' (target 'as a cloak'), a total garment-covering of disgrace they have earned. Here shame is invoked upon the enemy rather than endured by the self.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'dishonor (kelimmah)', and the type (102) is state. The bearer (105) is 'the accusers'. The operation (106) is 'be clothed with dishonor' — the garment-image again, disgrace put on like a robe: 'May my accusers be clothed with dishonor' (v29). The target (107) is 'before all': the clothing is public, disgrace displayed openly to everyone. The recorded coupling (112) and locus (116) values are cross-filed: the coupling flag reads 'internal:ib-state' while the locus value reads 'paired with the accusers and shame' — read for substance, the dishonor is an inner state welded to the bosheth 'shame' of the same verse (reading #sham#2), the two invoked together as a double covering. Source is not recorded (103 present:false): the dishonor is invoked, not traced to origin. Seat is 'none' (104). Manner is 'none' (108). Intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are absent (109/110/111/113): no degree, qualifier, consequence or prohibition. Role (115) is characteristic. The discovery (114) reads it as 'the disgrace invoked on the accusers, worn like a garment.' For the inner being, this dishonor is public disgrace called down as clothing — the accusers' interior standing stripped and re-dressed in humiliation for all to see. Preserving the distinction from the bosheth beside it (directive 8): the two words stack two overlapping images of the same imprecation, dishonor as a robe 'before all' and shame as an enveloping cloak, together burying the accusers under disgrace.
narratives.story: The prayer asks that the accusers be dressed in dishonour — disgrace hung on them like a garment, and worn out in the open where everyone can see. Right next to it stands the word for shame, wrapping them like a cloak, so they are covered twice: publicly dishonoured and personally shamed. The two images pile up, burying the men who tried to condemn the psalmist under the very disgrace they wished on him. Their standing is stripped away in full view. What they meant to pin on him is instead draped over them for all to witness.
narratives.variation_note: Against #1 (69:7), where kelimmah is the psalmist's own dishonor covering his face (self-suffered, seated on 'the face'), this reverses the bearer to 'the accusers' and the movement to imprecation: dishonor is called down and worn 'before all' (target), seat 'none'. Must also be held distinct from the paired bosheth 'shame' in the same verse (sham#2): the two words stack two overlapping garment-images of one imprecation — public dishonor as a robe, shame as an enveloping cloak.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'scorn (cherpah)', and the type (102) is state. The bearer (105) is 'the psalmist' — here cherpah falls on the sufferer himself, not on his foes. The operation (106) is 'be an object of scorn': the self is turned into a spectacle of contempt. The target (107) is 'to his accusers': the scorn is registered before the very people who accuse him, in the arena of their mockery. The recorded coupling (112) and locus (116) values are cross-filed: the coupling flag reads 'internal:ib-state' while the locus value reads 'paired with the wagging heads' — read for substance, the scorn is an inner state welded to a gesture, the accusers' wagging of the head ('when they see me, they wag their heads', v25), so the contempt and its bodily sign are one event. Source is not recorded (103 present:false): no origin traced at item level. Seat is 'none' (104). Manner is 'none' (108). Intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are absent (109/110/111/113): no degree, qualifier, consequence or prohibition. Role (115) is characteristic. The discovery (114) reads it as 'the psalmist's humiliation, mocked by his foes who wag their heads.' Set against the surrounding verse — knees weak from fasting, body gaunt (v24) — this scorn is the social crown on a bodily wasting: the self, already physically diminished, is made a public object of derision, its humiliation completed by the head-wagging contempt of onlookers. Read for the inner being, scorn is the wound of being reduced to a sight others shake their heads at.
narratives.story: The psalmist is already wasted thin — his knees weak from fasting, his body gaunt — and on top of that comes the humiliation: he has become a thing people sneer at. When his accusers see him, they shake their heads at him in contempt, and their scorn lands on a man already worn to nothing. His disgrace is completed by that mocking gesture, the wagging heads of people watching him suffer. He is not lashing out; he is simply the object of everyone's derision. It is the shame of being reduced to a pitiful sight for others to jeer at.
narratives.variation_note: The only reading of cherpah under the char_key 'scorn'; distinctive within the cherpah items in that the bearer is the psalmist himself (as in reproach#1/#2/#3) but the scorn is welded to a specific mocking gesture — the accusers' wagging heads — and set against a backdrop of bodily wasting (v24). It reads shame as social contempt crowning physical diminishment, rather than the God-borne reproach of 69:7/69:9 or the communal byword of 79:4.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'be put to shame (bosh)', and the type (102) is state. This is the ascent reading among the puttosham items: the bearer (105) is 'the psalmist', and the operation (106) is 'be (or not be) put to shame' — held in the negative: 'Then I shall NOT be put to shame, having my eyes fixed on all your commandments' (v6). The target (107) is 'before God/men': the (averted) shame belongs to the double arena of standing before God and before people. Coupling (112) binds it to 'the whole SHAME-arc of the psalm' — this single reading anchors every recurrence of the theme across Psalm 119 (vv31, 46, 80, 116), each a facet of one movement. Source is not recorded (103 present:false): no origin traced; the concern is aversion, not cause. Seat is 'none' (104) and locus (116) internal:ib-state. Manner is 'none' (108). Intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are absent (109/110/111/113 present:false): notably no prohibition is recorded even though the content is a guarding against shame — the not-being-shamed is framed as the psalmist's own characteristic outcome, not an external command. Role (115) is characteristic. The discovery (114) reads it as 'shame averted by fixing the eyes on the commandments.' For the inner being, this is shame defeated by orientation: the self that fixes its gaze on God's commandments is guarded from disgrace — the same mechanism as radiance (34:5), where the direction of attention pre-empts shame. Across the psalm the movement recurs as clinging to the testimonies (v31), bold speech before kings (v46), a blameless heart (v80), and unfailing hope (v116) — one interior kept from shame by adherence to the word.
narratives.story: In this long meditation on God's word, the psalmist keeps returning to one confidence: he will not be put to shame. The secret, he says, is where he keeps his eyes — fixed on God's commandments. As long as his gaze and his life are trained on the word, disgrace cannot settle on him, whether before God or before people. This same quiet assurance surfaces again and again through the psalm: he clings to God's testimonies, he speaks of them boldly even before kings, he asks that his heart be blameless, he rests his whole hope on the promise. It is one steady inner poise, a self kept from shame by holding fast to the word it loves.
narratives.variation_note: The sole ascent reading among the seven puttosham items: shame is not undergone or invoked but averted — the psalmist NOT put to shame (operation held in the negative) by fixing his gaze on the commandments, the self as bearer. It shares its mechanism with radiant (34:5): shame pre-empted by the direction of attention. Its four recurrences (119:31 clinging to the testimonies, 119:46 bold speech before kings, 119:80 a blameless heart, 119:116 unfailing hope) are facets of this one movement across Psalm 119, coupled explicitly to 'the whole SHAME-arc of the psalm'.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'be put to shame (bosh)', and the type (102) is state. Though the same root as puttosham, this item is filed under a distinct char_key ('put') and reads the descent pole within Psalm 119: the bearer (105) is 'the insolent' — the arrogant who 'smear me with lies' (v69) and 'wronged me with falsehood' (v78). The operation (106) is 'be (or not be) put to shame', here invoked upon the foes: 'Let the insolent be put to shame, because they have wronged me with falsehood' (v78). The target (107) is 'before God/men', the double arena of exposure. Coupling (112) binds it to 'the whole SHAME-arc of the psalm', tying this descent reading to the same overarching movement that #5 anchors from the ascent side. Source is not recorded (103 present:false): the shame is prayed for on the ground of their wrongdoing (stated in the discovery) but not traced as an item-level source. Seat is 'none' (104) and locus (116) internal:ib-state. Manner is 'none' (108). Intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are absent (109/110/111/113): no degree, qualifier, traced consequence or prohibition. Role (115) is characteristic. The discovery (114) reads it as 'the foes' shame invoked for their wrong.' For the inner being, this shame is disgrace called down as just recompense: the insolent who lied against the psalmist are asked to be humiliated in the same public arena where they slandered — while, in the same breath, the psalmist turns to meditate on God's precepts (v78b). The reading holds the two interiors together: the foe undone by shame for falsehood, the self steadied by the word.
narratives.story: The arrogant have smeared the psalmist with lies and wronged him with falsehood, and he prays that they be put to shame for it. Their disgrace is asked as a fair return — humiliation in the same public view where they slandered him. But notice what he does in the very same breath: he turns away from the quarrel to meditate on God's precepts. Two inner lives sit side by side here — the liars undone by the shame their falsehood earns, and the psalmist quietly settled in the word he loves. He leaves their downfall to God and steadies himself on something better.
narratives.variation_note: Same bosh root as the puttosham items but filed under a distinct char_key ('put'), and it reads the descent pole of Psalm 119: the bearer is 'the insolent', shame invoked on them for their falsehood, in direct contrast to puttosham#5 (119:6) where the psalmist himself is kept from shame. Both are coupled to 'the whole SHAME-arc of the psalm' (112), marking them the two poles — foe shamed / self guarded — of one movement running through Psalm 119.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'put to shame (bosh, negated)', and the type (102) is state. This is an ascent/vindication reading with a bearer unlike any other in the family: the bearer (105) is 'the man with children' — the father whose quiver is full of sons. The operation (106) is 'not be put to shame', held in the negative: 'He shall not be put to shame when he speaks with his enemies in the gate' (v5). The target (107) is 'before enemies at the gate' — the arena is the city gate, the place of legal dispute and public reckoning, where a man's standing is contested. The recorded coupling (112) and locus (116) values are cross-filed: the coupling flag reads 'internal:ib-state' while the locus value reads 'paired with the blessed man' — read for substance, the not-being-shamed is an inner state welded to the blessing pronounced on the man ('Blessed is the man who fills his quiver with them'), so his blessedness and his unshamable standing are one. Source is not recorded (103 present:false): the security is grounded in the gift of children (from the LORD, v3) but not traced as an item-level source. Seat is 'none' (104). Manner is 'none' (108). Intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are absent (109/110/111/113): no degree, qualifier, consequence or prohibition. Role (115) is characteristic. The discovery (114) reads it as 'the operation of vindicated standing: the man backed by sons is unashamed in the contest at the city gate.' For the inner being, this shame-averted state is confidence grounded in progeny: the interior of the father is fortified against public humiliation because he is backed, at the place of reckoning, by the sons God has given — shame pre-empted not by God's word (as in 119) but by God's gift of family.
narratives.story: This short psalm ends with a picture of a confident man. Because his home is full of children — sons given by God — he will not be put to shame when he stands at the city gate to face down those who oppose him. The gate is where disputes were settled and a man's standing was tested in public, and there he stands unshaken, backed by his family. His freedom from shame flows straight out of the blessing pronounced over him. Where other psalms guard against shame by clinging to God's word, here the shield against humiliation is the gift of a full house.
narratives.variation_note: An ascent/vindication puttosham reading with a unique bearer — 'the man with children' — and a unique ground: freedom from shame rests on the gift of sons, not (as in #5, 119:6) on fixing the gaze on God's word. Its arena is specific, 'before enemies at the gate' (the place of legal reckoning), and its not-being-shamed is welded to the blessing on the man. The data files coupling and locus with crossed values (coupling='internal:ib-state', locus='paired with the blessed man').

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'put to shame (bosh)', and the type (102) is state. The bearer (105) is 'the haters of Zion' — the enemies of God's city, the descent pole again. The operation (106) is 'be put to shame', a passive undergoing invoked by imprecation: 'May all who hate Zion be put to shame' (v5). The target (107) is 'and turned back': the shaming is joined to a rout — 'be put to shame and turned backward' — so disgrace and defeated retreat are one motion. The recorded coupling (112) and locus (116) values are cross-filed: the coupling flag reads 'internal:ib-state' while the locus value reads 'paired with the hatred of Zion' — read for substance, the shame is an inner state welded to the very hatred that provokes it, the haters' enmity turned back on itself as disgrace. Source is not recorded (103 present:false): the shame is prayed for, not traced to an origin. Seat is 'none' (104). Manner is 'none' (108). Intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are absent (109/110/111/113): no degree, qualifier, consequence or prohibition. Role (115) is characteristic. The discovery (114) reads it as 'the operation of the foes' collapse: the haters of Zion routed and shamed, like rooftop grass that withers.' For the inner being, this shame is the interior collapse of settled hostility: after a lifetime of afflicting Israel 'from my youth' (v1-2), the haters are asked to be shamed and driven back, their long enmity ending not in triumph but in a withering, disgraced retreat — the image of grass on the housetops that dies before it grows (v6) sealing the picture of a hostility that comes to nothing.
narratives.story: This pilgrim song remembers a lifetime of being attacked — 'from my youth they have afflicted me' — and ends with a prayer that the enemies of God's city be shamed and driven back. Their disgrace is tied to a rout: humiliated and turned around, sent packing. The hatred they nursed for so long is turned back on them as shame. The poem pictures them like grass that sprouts on a rooftop and withers before it ever grows tall — a hostility that comes to nothing. After all their afflicting, the haters simply collapse, disgraced, into failure.
narratives.variation_note: A descent/imprecatory puttosham reading with bearer 'the haters of Zion', where shame is joined to a rout — 'be put to shame and turned backward' (target 'and turned back') — after a lifetime of affliction (v1-2). It shares imprecatory shaming with #1 (83:17) but lacks the redemptive aim (their conversion); its logic is the collapse of long-settled hostility into a withering defeat. The data files coupling and locus with crossed values (coupling='internal:ib-state', locus='paired with the hatred of Zion').
